title: Funerals, societies and brass bands
summary: After a brief close of the sticks-arrest story, he explains that societies and clubs hired music for funerals, often several bands; Excelsior and the Onward were best, and undertakers now discourage music.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Not cool. Yeah, I was playing on this lady's step. And she said I used to know her, you see. So she had me arrested, see. So when I go to the judge, I could play the sticks pretty good, you know. So the judge said, well, can you play? I said, yeah, that's a good play so I played the job. And he said, well, this judge, man, he gave me 50 cents until I'm going home and don't do that no more. He said, don't play on that lady's step no more. I don't really tell you that one. How old were you? Oh, I was coming up, I was about, oh, I guess I was about 18, 12 or 18, somewhere around there. I can't recall anymore. I didn't keep them with all that, you know. And all that. Wow. Now you said, we're speaking about the dance halls, huh? Yeah, I was wondering, you know, what I mean? Well, about the funerals, you used to ask me about the, you asked me about the funerals? Well, at that particular time, I mean, those years, let's see, there had so many societies that used to turn out with music, you know, and everybody wanted to be buried by music, you know. So they joined these societies, you see, like the Young Men of our Day, the Old Men of our Day, the Liberty, and all so many, I can't recall all those. And even clubs, I mean, would give you music, like the Boots Club, the Lions Club, I mean, they gave you Masonics and all that, they'd have music. And sometimes, guys would belong to maybe three or four organizations that had, that would have music, you see. And, well, the widow would say, well, she wants music, and he wants music, that's what he wants, so he'd get the music. And they'd have, sometimes, three or four bands. Five of them went down and they had four bands.

And I can remember, two good bands, I mean, they had, that was Excelsior and the O.B.B.'s, the Armaid Brass Band. The O.B.B.'s was the best band, in my estimation. Not that my dad played with them, played with that band, but they actually had the best brass band. It was a radded brass band. It was more radded than, they played more radded music than Excelsior. Excelsior played a lot of marches, you know. All of them were good musicians. They were all good leaders. Yeah, that's it. But, I don't know, that would happen most any day they would bury somebody, you know.
Would it be Tuesday, Sunday, Saturday?
No, just any day, but most likely a guy would like to be held over on a Sunday, because everybody would be out to see a procession, you know, go by and see.
But they still did that until, that's quite recently, you know.
Yeah, recently, yeah, yeah. A few years back, I mean, they stopped that.
Well, Sunday's, the Undertaker's won't work on Sunday now, you know.

No, no, no. And then, the Undertaker don't care about your having in the music, because it takes too much time, you see, because the way people die so fast today is that they have time to make two or three funerals in one day, you see. Like, they have a body, they're taking about 8, burry, 8.30 in the morning, well, they have another 10.30, well, by that time, I mean, they're back, you see, they buried that person in that some other other person's house, you know, either back to the Undertaker, whatever, whatever he's laid off there, you know. And that would have a chance to bury, you know, two, three people. So, having music, it takes two more to play those marches, you know, a few more marches, you know.
